presenterNotes: Use physical cards or colored chips to demonstrate resampling: combine two groups, shuffle, and deal into new groups. Compute means and difference.
Emphasize the logic: if the treatment really had no effect, then the original group labels were arbitrary; resampling simulates all the ways the data could have been assigned.
Connect to the broader idea of hypothesis testing and p-values (though not named, the proportion of resampled differences beyond the observed is an empirical p-value).
title: Making Inferences from Experiments

teacherCues: Draw two dot plots on the board representing control and treatment group yields. Ask: 'How can we quantify the difference between these two groups?'
Introduce the formula: experimental difference = x̄_treatment − x̄_control. Emphasize that a positive difference suggests the treatment increased the outcome.

discoveryHook.scenario: A gardener wants to know if a new soil supplement really boosts tomato yield. She gives it to 10 plants and leaves 10 without. The difference in average yields might suggest the supplement works — but could the difference just be luck? To find out, we need a way to measure and test that difference.

examples.title: Example A – Music Therapy and Depression
examples.prompt: A study tests music therapy on depression scores (scale 20–80, >50 indicates depression). Control group (8 students): 49,45,43,47,46,45,47,46. Treatment group (8 students): 39,40,39,37,41,40,42,43. Find the experimental difference of means and interpret.
steps: Difference = 40.125 − 46 = −5.875, about −5.9 points.
Negative: the treatment group has a lower depression score, suggesting music therapy may reduce depression.

examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: If the difference is +3.2, which group had the higher average? Does this mean the treatment 'works'? Could it be just random variation?
examples.prompt: In a different experiment, the difference is +3.2. What does the sign tell you about the treatment?
examples.title: Example B – Interpreting Differences
steps: Positive difference → treatment mean > control mean.
The treatment group scored higher, but we don't yet know if 3.2 is a large enough difference to rule out chance.
Small sample sizes make it hard to tell; we need a method like resampling to see if 3.2 is unusual.

examples.title: Example C – Waist Circumference
examples.prompt: A laser therapy study has control group mean waist circumference 34.9 inches, treatment group mean 32.6 inches. Find the experimental difference and interpret.
steps: Difference = 32.6 − 34.9 = −2.3 inches.
The treatment group had a smaller average waist, a reduction of 2.3 inches.
Again, this is the observed effect; further analysis is needed to see if it's significant.

notes: A single number; does not yet tell us if the difference is statistically meaningful.
formulaCard.title: Experimental Difference of Means

explanation: A [[kw:randomized comparative experiment]] has at least two groups: a control group and one or more treatment groups.
A positive difference means the treatment group had a higher average; negative means lower; zero means no difference.
To visualize the data, use side‑by‑side dot plots or box plots. Look for overlap, symmetry, and outliers.
A small difference with a small sample size could easily happen by chance, even if the treatment has no effect.

questions.prompt: The experimental difference of means is found by subtracting the control group mean from the ___ group mean.
hints: Starts with 't'.
It's the group that receives the intervention.

questions.prompt: If x̄_control = 10 and x̄_treatment = 7, what is the experimental difference?
hints: Be careful with the sign.

questions.prompt: A positive experimental difference indicates the treatment ___ the measured outcome. (Answer 'increased' or 'decreased')
hints: Positive means treatment mean is larger.
Think of higher yield, higher score, etc.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Positive difference means the treatment increased the outcome.

confusionCorner.title: Sign of the Difference
confusionCorner.body: Always subtract in the same order: treatment − control. A negative number means the treatment reduced the measured quantity (like depression or waist size); a positive means it increased it (like yield or test scores). [[imp:Pay attention to the context!]]

blocks.title: Experiments with Two Samples

explanation: [[kw:Resampling]] is a method where the original data from both groups are combined, then repeatedly split at random into two new groups of the same sizes as the original.
For each resample, compute the difference of the means of the two new groups. This creates a [[kw:resampling distribution]] of differences.
The hypothesis we are testing is that the treatment has no effect, i.e., the true difference is 0.
The resampling distribution shows what differences occur by random chance alone. It is centered near 0.
If the original experimental difference is far out in the tail of this distribution, it suggests the difference is [[imp:unlikely to be due to chance alone]].

rows.1: Combine all measurements from both groups into one list.
Randomly draw a new 'control group' of the same size as the original, without replacement.
The remaining data form the new 'treatment group'.
Compute the difference: new treatment mean − new control mean.
Repeat many times (e.g., 200) and build a histogram of differences.

notes: The new groups are formed completely at random from the combined data.
This simulates a world where the treatment has no effect.
formulaCard.title: Resampling Difference

hints: Starts with 'r'.
It involves taking new samples from the original data.
questions.prompt: The process of repeatedly randomly reassigning data to groups to create a distribution of differences is called ___.
In resampling, the new groups are formed by drawing ___ replacement from the combined data. (Answer 'with' or 'without')
questions.feedbackIfWrong: We draw without replacement to preserve the data distribution.
hints: We don't want to use the same data point twice in one resample.
Think: each original value is used exactly once per resample.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The resampling distribution should be centered at 0.
hints: If treatment has no effect, true difference is 0.
The resampling process simulates that null hypothesis.
questions.prompt: What is the center of the resampling distribution of differences expected to be, assuming the treatment has no effect?

blocks.title: Resampling: Creating a Null Distribution
teacherCues: Write the hypothesis on the board: 'The treatment has no effect.' Explain that resampling simulates this 'no effect' world.
Demonstrate the resampling process using numbered cards or a random number generator: combine data, randomly assign to new groups, compute difference, repeat.

examples.title: Example A – Single Resample
steps: New treatment mean − new control mean = 1.57 − 1.49 = 0.08 kg.
This is much smaller than the original experimental difference of 0.32 kg.
This suggests the original difference of 0.32 might not occur often by chance.
examples.prompt: Combine the 10 control and 10 treatment tomato yields. Randomly draw 10 values for a new control group; the rest become new treatment. The new control mean is 1.49 kg, new treatment mean is 1.57 kg. What is the resampling difference?

examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: What would happen if we resampled with replacement? How does resampling preserve the original distribution of values?
examples.prompt: Why do we draw new groups without replacement from the combined data?
examples.title: Example B – Why Resample Without Replacement?
steps: We draw without replacement so each original data point is used exactly once per resample.
This preserves the overall distribution of the data while randomizing which group each value goes to.
If we drew with replacement, some values could appear multiple times, distorting the variability.

examples.title: Example C – Resampling the Music Therapy Data
examples.prompt: A researcher resamples the music therapy data 200 times. The histogram of resampling differences is approximately bell-shaped and centered at 0. The original experimental difference was −5.9. If −5.9 lies far in the left tail of the histogram, what does that suggest?
steps: The histogram shows differences that occur by chance if music therapy had no effect.
If −5.9 is far in the tail, it is a rare outcome under 'no effect'.
This provides evidence that music therapy might actually have an effect (reducing depression scores).

confusionCorner.body: Here we resample without replacement to simulate randomization under the null hypothesis. This is a permutation test. Bootstrapping, another resampling method, samples with replacement and is used for confidence intervals. They are related but have different goals.
confusionCorner.title: Resampling vs. Bootstrapping

discoveryHook.scenario: If the soil supplement really has zero effect, then any difference we saw between groups was just due to random assignment. Resampling mimics that: it shuffles the data, creates new fake 'treatment' and 'control' groups over and over, and shows what differences happen purely by chance.

After 200 resamplings, you see that differences as large as the one you observed (0.32 kg) occur only about 5% of the time by chance. That's rare! So you have strong evidence that the soil supplement really does boost tomato yield. The histogram tells the story.

blocks.title: Making Inferences from Resampling

examples.title: Example A – Tomato Supplement
examples.prompt: For the tomato experiment, the observed difference is 0.32. In 200 resamples, only about 8 differences were greater than 0.32 (4%). The middle 90% of differences ranged from −0.275 to 0.275. Should we reject 'no effect'?
steps: 0.32 is outside the middle 90% (which is −0.275 to 0.275).
Only about 4% of resampled differences are as large as 0.32, which is less than 5%.
We conclude the soil supplement does increase tomato yield.

examples.title: Example B – Not Significant
examples.prompt: Suppose the experimental difference was 0.15, and 35% of resampled differences were greater than 0.15. It lies within the central 90%. What do we conclude?
steps: 0.15 is not unusual — it falls in the range of typical chance differences.
We do not have enough evidence to say the treatment works.
We 'fail to reject' the no‑effect hypothesis; we don't prove the treatment has zero effect, only that we can't distinguish it from chance.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why don't we say 'the treatment has no effect'? Why do we say 'we fail to reject the hypothesis of no effect'?

examples.prompt: The music therapy experimental difference is −5.875. In 200 resamples, the middle 90% of differences is from −4.25 to 4.25, and −5.875 occurs in only 2% of resamples. What is your conclusion?
steps: −5.875 is outside the central 90% and occurs rarely (2% of the time).
This is strong evidence against 'no effect'.
We conclude that music therapy reduces depression scores.
examples.title: Example C – Music Therapy

confusionCorner.title: Fail to Reject vs. Accept
confusionCorner.body: We never 'accept' the hypothesis of no effect; we only 'fail to reject' it. There might be a small effect that our sample wasn't large enough to detect. [[imp:Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.]]

teacherCues: Display the histogram of 200 resampling differences from the tomato example. Draw a vertical line at the observed 0.32. Ask: 'What percent of resampled differences are at least this large?'
Explain the 5% threshold: if the observed difference lies outside the middle 95% of resampled differences, it's considered statistically significant.

questions.prompt: If the experimental difference lies outside the middle 90% of resampled differences, we ___ the hypothesis that the treatment has no effect.
hints: Starts with 'r'.
We conclude the treatment probably does have an effect.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: About 4% of resampled differences were larger, a rare outcome.
hints: The text said about 5 to 10 out of 200, which is at most 5%.
8 out of 200 is 4%.
questions.prompt: In the tomato example, what percentage of resampled differences were greater than the observed 0.32? (Approximate: 4, 15, or 50?)

hints: Center differences are common by chance.
We cannot distinguish the effect from random noise.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: No, a central difference is consistent with random variation; evidence is not strong.
questions.prompt: If an experimental difference falls near the center of the resampling distribution, do we have strong evidence that the treatment works? Answer 'yes' or 'no'.

formulaCard.title: Inference from Resampling
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If experimental difference is extreme relative to resampling distribution, conclude effect.} $$
notes: A common threshold: fewer than 5% of resampled differences are as extreme (or more extreme) than the observed.
The histogram should be approximately bell‑shaped.

rows.0: Outside the central 90% (or 95%) of resampled differences
rows.1: Reject 'no effect'; treatment has a significant effect.
Fail to reject 'no effect'; evidence of an effect is not strong enough.

explanation: After building a histogram of many resampling differences, compare the original experimental difference to this distribution.
If the experimental difference is in the far tail (e.g., beyond the central 90% or 95% of resampled differences), it's unlikely to occur by random chance alone.
In such cases, we [[imp:reject the hypothesis]] that the treatment has no effect, and conclude the treatment does have an effect.
The cutoff for 'unlikely' is often the central 90% or 95% of the resampling distribution (90% or 95% confidence).
If the experimental difference falls within the central region, we do not have enough evidence to reject the 'no effect' hypothesis.
1. [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the control and treatment groups, their sample sizes, and the hypothesis: 'The treatment has no effect.'
3. [[imp:Resample]]: Combine the data. Repeatedly (200+ times) randomly split into new groups of the original sizes. For each split, compute the new difference. Build a histogram.

4. [[imp:Conclude]]: Determine if the observed difference is in the tail of the histogram (e.g., outside the middle 90%). If yes, reject the 'no effect' hypothesis. If no, fail to reject. State your conclusion in context.

rows.2: Control n=8, treatment n=8. H₀: no effect on depression score.

rows.1: Combine, split randomly 200 times, record differences.
rows.2: Histogram of 200 resampling differences centered at 0.

rows.1: Is observed diff in tail? Reject or fail to reject H₀.
rows.2: −5.875 is far in left tail (rare) → reject H₀, music therapy reduces depression.

formulaCard.title: Resampling Blueprint Formula
notes: The p-value is the proportion of resampled differences as extreme as yours.
A p-value < 0.05 is commonly considered significant.
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If } P(\text{resampled diff} \ge |\text{observed diff}|) \text{ is small (< 0.05), reject } H_0. $$

discoveryHook.scenario: You've conducted a randomized experiment. Now what? The Resampling Blueprint takes you from data to decision in four clear steps, ensuring you don't mistake random chance for a real treatment effect.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Testing an Experiment with Resampling

examples.prompt: Laser therapy study: control mean = 34.9 in., treatment mean = 32.6 in., n=8 each. After 200 resamples, the middle 90% of differences is (−2.1, 2.1). The observed difference is −2.3. What do you conclude?
examples.title: Example A – Full Blueprint for Waist Circumference
steps: Understand: H₀: laser therapy has no effect on waist size. Observed diff = −2.3.
Observe: −2.3 is outside (−2.1, 2.1), so it is in the tail.
Resample: The histogram shows differences outside ±2.1 are rare.
Conclude: Reject H₀. There is evidence laser therapy reduces waist circumference.

examples.title: Example B – When the Difference Is Not Extreme
steps: −1.0 is not extreme; it falls in the range of typical chance differences.
We fail to reject H₀: there is not enough evidence to say the therapy works.
This doesn't prove it has zero effect; the sample might be too small to detect a small true effect.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: If −1.0 is common under the resampling distribution, what does that mean? Why can't we claim the therapy works?
examples.prompt: Suppose the waist difference was −1.0, well inside (−2.1, 2.1). How would the conclusion change?

examples.title: Example C – Your Turn
examples.prompt: An experiment tests a new study app. Control mean test score = 75, treatment mean = 82, n=15 each. After 200 resamples, the histogram of differences is approximately normal with middle 90% from −6 to +6. Observed difference = +7. What is your conclusion?
steps: Observed diff = 82 − 75 = +7, which is outside (−6,6).
This falls in the tail, so it's unlikely due to chance.
Reject H₀; the study app appears to improve test scores.

teacherCues: Write the blueprint steps: 1) Understand the experiment and state the 'no effect' hypothesis. 2) Compute the experimental difference. 3) Resample many times and build a histogram. 4) Compare and conclude.
Model the process with the music therapy data, from start to finish.

confusionCorner.body: Resampling only works if you generate enough resamples (at least 100–200). A single resample tells you nothing. The histogram reveals the distribution of chance differences.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Skip the Histogram
